title: Paloma and the Weather
premise: Mara Eriksen, a piano tuner who reads the past in the sounds of old houses, has spent forty years as a guest in his own life, drifting between jobs, rooms, and other people's families. When the house on Vell Street—the childhood home he fled at nineteen after the night no one will name—goes up for auction, Mara returns to tune the piano one last time and finds himself unable to leave. As the sale date approaches, his siblings converge with their own versions of the family story, and Mara must finally ask the question they all arranged their silences around: what happened to their mother on the night she walked into the storm and never came back. The novel ends not with an answer that absolves anyone, but with Mara buying back a single room of the house—and, for the first time, owning his place inside the family's unfinished weather.
about_author: Emrys Thackeray is the pen name of a former piano restorer who spent two decades listening to houses before writing about them. Paloma and the Weather is his second novel, written in a rented cottage whose radiators he refuses to fix.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Ear
chapters.summary: Mara tunes a grand piano in a stranger's mansion, narrating the house's history through its creaks and radiator knocks. POV: Mara. Establishes his gift for hearing what buildings remember and his habit of leaving before he's asked to stay. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: Tenant
chapters.summary: In his furnished sublet, Mara eats off a landlord's plates and rehearses polite exits. A letter arrives from a law firm: the Vell Street house enters probate auction in six weeks. POV: Mara. He almost throws the letter away. Emotional beat: dread surfacing beneath practiced detachment.

chapters.title: Vell Street, 1979
chapters.summary: A memory chapter: young Mara under the piano while rain hammers the roof, his mother Paloma playing Chopin badly and beautifully, his father's boots on the stairs. POV: Mara (past). The warmth before the wound. Emotional beat: nostalgia sharpened by the reader's knowledge that something broke.

chapters.title: The Auction Notice
chapters.summary: Mara travels to his hometown ostensibly to appraise the piano for the estate sale. The realtor, Dee, mistakes him for a buyer; he doesn't correct her. POV: Mara. Walking the empty rooms, he hears the house holding its breath. Emotional beat: the pull of return he can't rationalize.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Said
chapters.summary: Alone overnight in the house, Mara maps its sounds—the radiator knock his father called 'the argument,' the whistle in the stairwell where Paloma used to sing. POV: Mara. He realizes the house kept records the family refused to. Emotional beat: grief arriving as acoustics.

chapters.title: Sister, With Keys
chapters.summary: His sister Ingrid arrives unannounced, holding the estate keys and a ledger of grievances. She assumes he's here to claim a share and warns him not to 'make it a thing.' POV: alternating Mara/Ingrid. Their friction reveals how differently each survived childhood. Emotional beat: sibling love expressed as suspicion.

chapters.title: The Brother Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Oldest brother Tomas, who never left town, meets Mara at the hardware store and pretends it's coincidence. Over coffee he says the unsayable: 'You got to leave. Somebody had to stay and be blamed.' POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: resentment curdling into confession-adjacent honesty.

chapters.title: Paloma's Room
chapters.summary: Mara opens the sealed bedroom. Dust, a half-finished scarf, sheet music annotated in her hand—a waltz titled 'For the Weather.' POV: Mara. He plays the fragment on the out-of-tune upright and the house answers. Emotional beat: intimacy with the dead, and the first crack in his silence.

chapters.title: Dee's Offer
chapters.summary: Realtor Dee, herself raised in foster care, tells Mara she'd give anything for a house with ghosts. She offers to delay listing so he can 'sort things out,' asking nothing in return—which terrifies him more than pressure would. POV: Dee. Emotional beat: kindness as confrontation.

chapters.title: The Night, Version One
chapters.summary: Flashback filtered through Tomas's account: the storm, the shouting, Paloma walking out with an umbrella she left open on the porch. POV: Tomas. His version casts fourteen-year-old Mara as the cause—he'd broken the piano bench, started the fight. Emotional beat: guilt weaponized.

chapters.title: Auction Preview
chapters.summary: Strangers wander the house appraising Paloma's belongings. Mara watches a woman buy his mother's teacups and nearly intervenes. Ingrid arrives to stage the rooms and finds him sitting in the dark. POV: Mara. Emotional beat: the horror of a life becoming inventory.

chapters.title: Version Two
chapters.summary: Ingrid's account over wine: Paloma didn't vanish—she chose to go, and wrote to Ingrid for years afterward, letters Ingrid hid to protect everyone, especially Mara. POV: Ingrid. Emotional beat: betrayal reframed as protection, and the question of who gets to decide what others can bear.

chapters.title: Letters, Unsent and Otherwise
chapters.summary: Mara confronts Ingrid; she surrenders a shoebox. The letters are warm, evasive, alive—Paloma in another city, another name, asking about 'the boy who listens to pipes.' POV: Mara. He learns he was loved and lied to in the same breath. Emotional beat: rage and relief tangled.

chapters.title: The Question Beneath the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Mara stops tuning work entirely and sits with the house, composing the question he must ask: not where did she go, but why did we all agree to let her go without following? POV: Mara. He drafts and burns three letters to his siblings. Emotional beat: the stillness before rupture.

chapters.title: Convergence
chapters.summary: Tomas, Ingrid, and Mara meet in the kitchen to sign final sale papers. Instead Mara asks his question aloud. The room detonates: Tomas's guilt, Ingrid's secrets, Mara's abandonment—all laid on the table like the auction lots upstairs. POV: rotating among the three. Emotional beat: climax; the family's architecture collapses into truth.

chapters.title: What Paloma Left Out
chapters.summary: Among the letters, Mara finds one addressed to him, never sent: Paloma explaining that she left because staying meant teaching her children to disappear, as she had. She named the letter 'For the Weather.' POV: Mara reading. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness; the answer was always addressed to him.

chapters.title: Bidding War
chapters.summary: Auction day. Developers circle; the price climbs past what any sibling can pay alone. Mara, who has never bid on anything in his life, raises his hand—not for the house, but for one lot: the upright piano. POV: Mara. Emotional beat: public vulnerability; choosing presence over ownership.

chapters.title: One Room
chapters.summary: The house sells. But Mara negotiates with the buyer—a young couple charmed by his stories—to keep access to the music room, which he'll restore and maintain. Tomas offers money without being asked; Ingrid brings the shoebox to live there. POV: Mara. Emotional beat: belonging redefined as participation, not possession.

chapters.title: Tuning For the Weather
chapters.summary: Mara restores the upright and finishes Paloma's waltz using her annotations, playing it for Tomas and Ingrid in the sold house that still knows them. POV: Mara. The radiator knocks sound, for once, like applause. Emotional beat: mourning transmuted into music.

chapters.title: Dee's Key
chapters.summary: Dee helps Mara find a small apartment he'll actually sign a lease on—two years, unfurnished, his own plates. She asks what changed. He says: 'I stopped waiting to be evicted from my own story.' POV: Dee observing Mara. Emotional beat: quiet hope; roots planted deliberately.

chapters.title: The House Remembers Differently Now
chapters.summary: Months later, Mara visits the new family on Vell Street, tuning their piano as a favor. The children show him the whistle in the stairwell; he teaches them to hear it as a song. POV: Mara. Emotional beat: continuity—the gift passed on, the past made hospitable.

chapters.title: Coda: Open Umbrella
chapters.summary: Final scene: Mara on his own balcony in the rain, umbrella deliberately open beside him, mail on his table bearing his name at a real address. He hums the finished waltz. POV: Mara. The question answered not in words but in staying. Emotional beat: resolution—an owned life, however small, however weathered.
